title: Customer briefing: ingress queue latency surge — recovery options & verification
body:
TL;DR: On 2029-10-02 18:17 UTC a sustained latency surge impacted the ingress queue in our eu-west region for ~2 hours, causing delayed responses and increased timeouts for some customer requests. We implemented a graduated mitigation (priority drain + temporary rate-limits + regional redeploy) which restored normal throughput by 20:45 UTC. This doc outlines the customer-facing statuspage blurb, a succinct post-incident summary you can share with stakeholders, verification steps customers can run, reconciliation/replay options, and our next steps including compensation and technical remediation.

Statuspage draft (short):
- Incident start: 2029-10-02 18:17 UTC
- Impact: Elevated request latency and intermittent timeouts for API calls routed through eu-west ingress. Affected tenants saw delayed responses and occasional 5xx errors.
- Status: Service restored (partial recovery at 19:50 UTC, full recovery at 20:45 UTC). Rollforward completed; no customer data loss.
- Next update: post-incident summary (ETA 2029-10-04).

Customer executive summary (1–2 paragraphs):
On 2029-10-02 we detected an unexpected spike in request latency originating in our ingress queue subsystem in eu-west. The root trigger was a pathological interaction between a backlog of small requests and a new scheduling heuristic in the regional router that temporarily prevented effective draining of long-lived KV-cache warming operations. This produced queue head-of-line blocking and contributed to elevated P95/P99 latencies for ~2 hours. We prioritized a safe rollback of the scheduling heuristic and applied a targeted regional restart of the ingress fleet, followed by a controlled backlog drain. Normal service has been restored. We have not observed any unauthorized access or customer data loss.

Customer-facing timeline (concise):
- 18:17 UTC: Automated alerts triggered for increased P99 latency and queue depth.
- 18:20–18:40 UTC: Ops team began investigation; mitigation options evaluated.
- 18:45 UTC: Temporary tenant-level rate limits engaged to reduce new work entering queue.
- 19:05 UTC: Rollback of scheduling heuristic started for affected hosts.
- 19:30 UTC: Controlled regional restart of ingress workers initiated.
- 19:50 UTC: Majority of tenants showing latency improvement; partial recovery announced.
- 20:45 UTC: Final verification completed; system observed within normal baselines.

Root cause (plain language):
A recent change to the regional router scheduling heuristic (deployed 2029-09-29) increased affinity for cache-warming operations to co-reside on certain ingress workers. Under a burst of small requests, these workers experienced sustained KV-cache warmups that prevented the scheduler from rebalancing work efficiently. The effect: head-of-line blocking inside the regional ingress queue and slow consumer throughput.

Customer impact specifics:
- Symptoms: Increased P95/P99 latency (text-generation and embeddings endpoints most visible), occasional 502/504 responses for retries that hit the overloaded ingress worker.
- Scope: ~3% of overall tenants routed through eu-west between 18:17–20:45 UTC experienced degraded latency or brief request failures. Large enterprise tenants with sustained high-concurrency workloads were more likely to be affected.
- Data integrity: There is no evidence of lost or corrupted data. All accepted requests are persisted; timeouts in client are the primary failure mode.

Verification steps for customers (self-service):
1) Confirm your tenant metrics: check request latency and error rate for eu-west between 18:00–21:00 UTC. Look for elevated P99 and a spike in 5xx responses.
2) Re-run a small sample of representative calls (non-destructive) against the same model pins and compare latencies to pre-incident baselines.
3) If you took client-side defensive measures (circuit breakers, reduced concurrency), re-evaluate and baseline traffic gradually to original concurrency levels.
4) If you need a signed evidence bundle (timestamps, traces, request IDs), open a support ticket referencing INCIDENT-4821 and include a preferred time window for delivery.

Replay and reconciliation options (customer choices):
- Option A (no action): If you experienced only transient timeouts with minimal business impact, no action required.
- Option B (targeted replay): We can replay accepted requests that returned 5xx where the server-side logs indicate request ingestion but no completion. This requires customer opt-in and may take up to 72 hours to prepare an evidence bundle and run replay in a controlled environment.
- Option C (bulk reconciliation): For customers who rely on deterministic inference (e.g., index generation), we offer a reconciliation run at reduced throughput for a mutually agreeable maintenance window. Note: results can differ if models or pins changed since the incident.

How to request replays/evidence:
- Open a ticket via your account manager or support portal with subject: "INC-4821 evidence/replay request" and include tenant_id, timeframe, and preferred SLAs.
- We will provide an evidence package (traces, request IDs, ingestion confirmation) and a recommended replay plan. Replays require tenant consent and may incur usage charges unless otherwise agreed.

Immediate customer mitigations we recommend:
- Short-term: Add exponential backoff with jitter for retries and prefer idempotent request patterns where possible.
- Mid-term: Use conservative client-side concurrency limits during deployments or regional abnormalities.
- If you use long-running streaming sessions, consider layered keepalive pings to detect early pathologies and failover to alternate regions if critical.

Internal remediation and timeline:
- Short-term (complete): rollback scheduling heuristic (done), ingress fleet restart (done), enhanced alerting for queue-head blocking (done).
- Medium-term (2–4 weeks): revise scheduling heuristic to account for KV-cache warmups, add throttling guardrails, and expand synthetic traffic tests that emulate heavy small-request bursts.
- Long-term (2–3 months): improve routing simulation and add tenant-level isolation modes that prevent one tenant workload from impacting ingress worker scheduling.

SLA and compensation:
- If you believe SLA credits apply, please open a billing-SLA claim. We will correlate your tenant impact window and follow standard SLA credit procedures. We will proactively reach out to customers with measurable impact > 1% of requests during the window.

FAQ / anticipated customer Qs:
Q: Was my data exposed? A: No evidence of unauthorized access. All logs indicate normal access controls.
Q: Will replays change model outputs? A: Replays attempt to reproduce the original request state, but results may differ if model weights, temperature, tokenization, or pin versions have changed since the incident.
Q: How do I avoid similar issues? A: Follow the mitigation guidance above and enroll in our tenant resilience review for high-concurrency customers.

Next steps for us (customer-success + ops coordination):
- Publish statuspage brief now with incident summary and expected postmortem date (owner: Ava).
- Draft detailed post-incident report for customers with curated evidence bundle (owner: Liam).
- Outreach to customers with >5% request impact to offer concierge replay and credits discussion (owner: Sofia).

Notes to self / internal items to finish in doc:
- Add targeted example support ticket template for replays (include fields and consent checkbox).
- Attach anonymized sample trace illustrating head-of-line blocking.
- Confirm list of affected tenants and ensure PM/sales outreach is aligned.

Contact for customers: support@redwood.ai (priority ops channel) or your account manager. For internal follow-up: slack #inc-4821 and confluence page linked above.
